catalog_quote: Accent is distinctive in the language as words are contrasted according to the particular syllable on which accent is placed. There are a number of minimal pairs which contrast solely through accent placement. In the following examples, the first set of disyllabic words have the accent on the first syllable whilst the second set have it on the second syllable: tabo 'snake' tabó 'neck' ... What exactly is meant by 'accent'? There is no consensus amongst linguists who have worked on the language as to what feature or bundle of features mark the 'accent'. Bartos (1977) refers to the feature as 'stress' but fails to characterize or define it. McConvell (1983) refers to it as 'pitch-accent' with the accented syllable being the one carrying high tone/stress on it. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Piper 1989 text we hold layer and PDF (sec. 1.3, pp. 28-30; intro p.14; verb-chapter stress-shift note thesis p.93/p.105). Only nit: thesis pagination is 16-18, not 15-17. (2) Deciding source: a 224-leaf ANU MA-thesis sketch grammar (1989; LINCOM reprint 2013) with its own pitch accent section that explicitly reviews the competing analyses (Bartos 'stress', McConvell 'pitch accent', Rigsby p.c.). Against Glottolog's list (otherwise 1877-1907 sketches plus a 4-pp 1984 newsletter note) it is clearly the best available; WALS uses the same source. No post-1989 phonology/prosody study could be found in Glottolog, WALS, Piper's bibliography or Wikipedia's reference list
